title: Deadlocks and Deadlock Graphs
description: Learn what deadlocks are, how SQL Server detects them, how to read deadlock graphs, and how to design your way out of recurring deadlocks.

data.text: A **deadlock** is the ultimate concurrency problem: two (or more) sessions are each waiting for a resource the other holds, and neither can move forward. SQL Server resolves deadlocks automatically by choosing a victim — one session is rolled back and its locks are released so the other can continue. The victim receives error 1205.

Deadlocks are not bugs. They are a natural consequence of concurrent access. However, frequent deadlocks in production are a design smell. They indicate that your transactions are touching the same objects in inconsistent order, or that your isolation level allows too much overlap.
The Four Conditions for a Deadlock
For a deadlock to occur, all four of these conditions must be true at the same time. This is known as Coffman's conditions. If you can break even one of them, deadlocks cannot form.

data.title: Coffman's Conditions
items: Mutual Exclusion — at least one resource cannot be shared (e.g., an exclusive lock)
Hold and Wait — a session holds one resource while waiting for another
No Preemption — SQL Server cannot forcibly take a lock from a session; it must wait for the session to release it
Circular Wait — a chain of sessions exists where each is waiting for the next, and the last is waiting for the first

data.text: How SQL Server Detects and Resolves Deadlocks

SQL Server runs a background deadlock detector thread that periodically checks for cycles in the lock wait graph. When a deadlock is detected, SQL Server chooses a victim based on cost: the session with the lowest rollback cost is killed. You can influence which session survives by setting the `DEADLOCK_PRIORITY` session option.

data.caption: A classic deadlock: Session A holds Resource 1 and waits for Resource 2, while Session B holds Resource 2 and waits for Resource 1.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Session A] -->|holds| R1[Resource 1]
    A -->|waits for| R2[Resource 2]
    B[Session B] -->|holds| R2
    B -->|waits for| R1
    R1 -.->|blocked by| A
    R2 -.->|blocked by| B

data.text: SQL Server can write deadlock graphs to the error log or Extended Events session. A deadlock graph shows each process (session), the resources it holds, the resources it is waiting for, and the final victim chosen. Reading a deadlock graph is a detective skill: you need to find the exact statements and resources involved to fix the root cause.

data.title: Reading a Deadlock Graph XML
data.content: When deadlocks are captured via Extended Events or the error log, the XML shows processes, resources, and the victim. Here is a simplified example of what to look for.
data.code:
<deadlock>
  <victim-list>
    <victimProcess id="process2" />
  </victim-list>
  <process-list>
    <process id="process1" ...>
      <executionStack>
        <frame procname="dbo.UpdateOrder" line="12" sqlhandle="...">
          UPDATE Orders SET Status = 'Shipped' WHERE OrderId = 1001;
        </frame>
      </executionStack>
    </process>
    <process id="process2" ...>
      <executionStack>
        <frame procname="dbo.UpdateCustomer" line="8" sqlhandle="...">
          UPDATE Customers SET LastOrderId = 1001 WHERE CustomerId = 500;
        </frame>
      </executionStack>
    </process>
  </process-list>
  <resource-list>
    <keylock hobtid="..." dbid="7" objectname="dbo.Orders" indexname="PK_Orders">
      <owner-list>
        <owner id="process1" mode="X" />
      </owner-list>
      <waiter-list>
        <waiter id="process2" mode="X" requestType="wait" />
      </waiter-list>
    </keylock>
  </resource-list>
</deadlock>

data.title: Enable Deadlock Tracking
data.text: Always enable the system_health Extended Events session (it is on by default in modern SQL Server versions) or create a custom deadlock graph trace. Without data, you cannot fix what you cannot see.

You cannot eliminate deadlocks entirely in a high-concurrency system, but you can drastically reduce them. The most effective strategies are: access objects in a consistent order, keep transactions short, use lower isolation levels where possible, and add appropriate indexes to reduce lock duration.

data.title: Deadlock Prevention Strategies
items: Access tables in the same order across all procedures — if Procedure A updates Orders then Customers, Procedure B should not update Customers then Orders
Keep transactions as short as possible — do not include user think time, API calls, or long computations inside a transaction
Use `READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT` or `SNAPSHOT` isolation to eliminate reader-writer blocking where appropriate
Add covering indexes so that UPDATE and DELETE statements touch as few rows and pages as possible
Set `DEADLOCK_PRIORITY LOW` for non-critical sessions so they are chosen as victims instead of important ones
Avoid user-defined transactions in application code when the ORM or data access layer can manage them automatically

data.title: Design Tip
data.text: The single most impactful deadlock prevention technique is consistent access order. If every piece of code touches table A before table B, circular waits become structurally impossible.

items.question: Should I retry when error 1205 occurs?
items.answer: Yes. Error 1205 is a normal concurrency event, not a catastrophic failure. Applications should catch error 1205 and retry the transaction with a short backoff. Microsoft recommends retrying three to five times.

items.question: Does setting DEADLOCK_PRIORITY LOW eliminate deadlocks?
items.answer: No. It only controls which session is chosen as the victim when a deadlock occurs. The underlying deadlock still happens. Use priority to protect critical workloads, not as a substitute for fixing root causes.

items.question: Can monitoring tools see every deadlock?
items.answer: The system_health session captures deadlocks, but it samples data and may miss extremely short deadlocks in very busy systems. For critical environments, create a dedicated Extended Events session with a larger ring buffer or target file.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: A deadlock is a circular wait where two or more sessions hold resources each other needs
SQL Server automatically resolves deadlocks by choosing a victim — the session with the lowest rollback cost
Deadlock graphs reveal the exact statements, resources, and victim; reading them is essential for root-cause analysis
Consistent access order, short transactions, and appropriate indexes are the most effective prevention strategies
Error 1205 should be handled with retries in application code, not treated as a production emergency
data.takeaway: Deadlocks are inevitable in concurrent systems, but with consistent ordering and short transactions, they become rare events rather than production incidents.
